lessons.title: What “supervisor” means on an Alberta work site
lessons.html:
This course is for people who lead a small team, fill in as a lead hand, or want to work better with others at work. It is not an HR course. It does not teach you how to hire, fire, or discipline someone. It is not legal advice.

Alberta’s occupational health and safety (OHS) law uses the idea of an internal responsibility system. The Government of Alberta says every person on a work site is responsible for working toward a healthy and safe workplace, and every work site party is accountable for workplace health and safety.

In OHS language, a supervisor is a person who is in charge of a work site or has authority over one or more workers. The title on a name badge is not what decides this. If you tell other people what to do, or you are in charge of a site, Alberta’s supervisor duties can apply to you.

An employer includes a person who employs or engages one or more workers. Employers must make sure workers are supervised by supervisors who are competent and familiar with the OHS rules that apply to the work. They must also make workers aware of their rights and responsibilities under OHS legislation.

A worker is any person engaged in an occupation. That can include a volunteer who performs or supplies services for an organization or employer. Some people, such as unpaid students in a learning activity, are not considered workers on that page.

If you are unsure who the supervisor is on your site, ask your employer. If something feels unsafe, you can also contact the OHS Contact Centre. As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Alberta listed 780-415-8690 in Edmonton and toll free 1-866-415-8690.

lessons.title: Supervisor and worker health-and-safety duties
lessons.html:
Everyone on a work site has duties. This lesson names the ones Alberta lists for supervisors and workers. It does not replace the official guide or the law.

Supervisors are responsible for:

  • protecting the health and safety of the workers they supervise
  • making sure those workers work in a healthy and safe manner, follow OHS legislation, and are not subject to or participating in harassment and violence
  • advising their workers of all known or reasonably foreseeable work hazards
  • reporting health and safety concerns and conditions to their employer
  • cooperating with any person who is exercising a duty under the OHS legislation

If you supervise people, a plain way to remember this is: tell people about hazards you know or can reasonably foresee, help them work safely, do not ignore harassment or violence, and tell your employer when something is wrong.

Workers also have duties. They must protect their own health and safety and that of others at or near the work site. They must cooperate with their employer or supervisor by following the health and safety rules for the job. They must use hazard controls and wear the personal protective equipment the employer designates or the law requires. They must not cause or take part in harassment and violence. They must report health and safety concerns to their employer or supervisor, take part in training the employer provides, and cooperate with anyone exercising an OHS duty.

ALIS, a Government of Alberta site, adds that supervisors should take action to protect workers, including from violence and harassment, make sure people can do the work safely, and report concerns to the right people.

These duties go both ways. A supervisor who only “gives orders” and never listens to a safety concern is not meeting the official picture.

lessons.title: Workers’ rights and refusing dangerous work
lessons.html:
ALIS says workers have three fundamental health and safety rights under Alberta’s Occupational Health and Safety Act:

  1. The right to refuse unsafe work
  2. The right to know about workplace hazards
  3. The right to participate in health and safety decisions

The right to know means workers should be told about hazards and about what is being done to control or eliminate them. The right to participate means workers can take part in decisions that affect their health and safety. Many workplaces have a health and safety committee or a representative who speaks for workers.

The official OHS page “Refuse dangerous work” explains the right to refuse in more detail. Workers on provincially regulated work sites can refuse work if they reasonably think there is an undue hazard. An undue hazard is a serious and immediate threat to health and safety that the refusing worker actually observes or experiences at the work site.

Workers are protected from reprisal for exercising this right. Employers cannot take or threaten disciplinary action against a worker for exercising their rights and duties under the legislation.

If you refuse work you think is dangerous:

  1. Do not do that work.
  2. Tell your employer, supervisor, or another designated person as soon as you can what you are refusing and why.
  3. As much as possible, make sure your refusal does not endanger others.
  4. Your employer must look into the hazard and take action.
  5. You can do other work your employer assigns if you can reasonably do it and it is safe.

If your employer will not stop work you think is dangerous, contact the OHS Contact Centre (1-866-415-8690 as of 10 November 2026, America/Regina). This course cannot decide a real refusal for you.

lessons.title: Employment standards pointers, not HR advice
lessons.html:
Health and safety rules are not the only official rules at work. Employment standards set out rights and obligations of employers and employees in Alberta, including minimum standards employers must provide. The Alberta Employment Standards page is the starting map. It points to rules about minimum wage, overtime, holidays, leaves, vacations, hours of work, earnings, youth workers, and termination. This course does not teach those topics in full, and it does not tell you what to pay someone.

One page many new supervisors look up is “Hours of work and rest.” As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), that page said:

  • An employee’s work must stay within 12 consecutive hours a day, unless an exception applies (for example, an accident, urgent work, or a variance).
  • For a shift of more than 5 hours but less than 10 hours, the employee is entitled to at least one 30-minute break.
  • For a shift of 10 hours or more, the employee is entitled to two 30-minute breaks.
  • A shift of 5 hours or less has no break entitlement on that page.
  • Employees are entitled to at least one day of rest each work week.

The same page lists exceptions and exempt occupations, including managers, supervisors, and people employed in a confidential capacity. If your role is called “supervisor,” do not guess which rules apply. Read the live page. If the page differs from the legislation, Alberta says the legislation is considered correct.

To ask a question, use the official contact page. As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Employment Standards listed 780-427-3731 in the Edmonton area and toll free 1-877-427-3731 in Alberta. Online questions receive a response within 3 business days. That form cannot be used to make a complaint.

lessons.title: Skills for working with people, including leading a small group
lessons.html:
Safety rules and employment standards tell you what the law expects. Day-to-day work also depends on how people treat one another. Canada’s Skills for Success describe skills that help you at work, in learning, and in life. Two skills matter a great deal when you supervise or work beside others: collaboration and communication.

Collaboration is your ability to contribute and support others to achieve a common goal. The official components include:

  • working well with other people, such as being on time and encouraging cooperative behaviour
  • valuing diversity and inclusivity, and responding without judging people for different opinions
  • managing difficult interactions in a sensitive and helpful way
  • acknowledging the roles of yourself and others
  • supporting others through coaching, mentoring, and motivating
  • taking responsibility for your own tasks, sharing information, and making sure others have a chance to contribute
  • reflecting on how the team did and using feedback in a constructive way

Skills for Success does not list a separate skill called “leadership.” Supporting others through coaching, mentoring, and motivating is part of collaboration. That is the official leadership pointer in this course.

Communication is your ability to receive, understand, consider, and share information by speaking, listening, and interacting. Useful parts include listening with attention, asking questions to confirm what you heard, speaking clearly and with a purpose, and adapting your words to the people you are talking with.

These skills help a lead hand or new supervisor work with people. They do not replace OHS or employment standards, and they do not make you an HR manager. Practise them at work, and check official pages when a safety or pay question comes up.
